concept-cognition.def: A mental category that groups similar objects, events, ideas or people, such as "bird" or "fruit".

prototype.def: The best or most typical example of a concept, used to judge whether new things belong. A robin is a prototype bird.

assimilation.def: Interpreting new information so it fits an existing schema, as when a child calls a cow a "dog".

accommodation.def: Changing a schema, or creating a new one, when new information does not fit, as when the child learns that cows are not dogs.

algorithm.def: A step-by-step procedure that guarantees a solution if followed, often slowly, such as trying every possible code.

heuristic.def: A mental shortcut that allows fast judgments and solutions. Heuristics usually work but can lead to errors.

representativeness.def: Judging how likely something is by how well it matches a prototype, often ignoring how common it is.

availability.def: Judging how likely or common something is by how easily examples come to mind. Vivid, recent events seem more common than they are.

mental-set.def: The tendency to approach a problem in a way that worked before, even when another approach would work better.

functional-fixedness.def: The tendency to see an object only in its usual function, which blocks seeing new uses for it.

priming.def: The activation, often without awareness, of related ideas by an earlier exposure, so that later related items come to mind faster.

framing.def: The way a choice is worded (for example as a gain or a loss) changing the decision, even when the facts are the same.

gamblers-fallacy.def: The belief that past random outcomes change the chances of the next one, such as thinking black is "due" after a run of reds.

sunk-cost.def: Continuing a choice because of what has already been invested (money, time, effort) that cannot be recovered.

executive-functions.def: Mental skills for planning, focusing, switching between tasks and controlling impulses. They depend heavily on the prefrontal cortex.

creativity.def: The ability to produce ideas that are both new and useful.

divergent-thinking.def: Thinking that produces many different possible answers or ideas, such as listing uses for a brick.

convergent-thinking.def: Thinking that narrows the possibilities to one best answer, as on a test with a single right answer.
